sections.title: Greet: choose the right question
body: In Finland, Hej is the everyday greeting everywhere: in shops, at work, and with friends. Finland-Swedish speakers often say Hej hej, and in southern Finland you will also hear the informal Morjens.
The everyday check-in is Hur är det? or Hur är det med dig? (How are things with you?). Very casual friends say Läget? or Hur är läget? (What's up?).
Hur mår du? asks more personally how someone feels. Friends use it too, and it is the natural question when someone has been ill or tired: Mår du bättre nu?

sections.title: How are you? Pick an honest answer
body: Whichever question you hear, a short answer is enough: Bra, tack. Och du? You do not need to tell your whole day to someone you barely know.
Answer with the verb you hear: Hur är det? → Det är bra. Hur mår du? → Jag mår bra. You will also hear Jag är bra in casual speech, and Bara bra (just fine).
Then send the question back with Och du?, the same move you learned in Lesson 1.

sections.title: Pronouns: point to people without names
body: Swedish subject pronouns: jag (I), du (you, one person), han (he), hon (she), hen (they, one person), vi (we), ni (you, two or more), de (they).
English has one word, you. Swedish counts the people: du is singular (one person), ni is plural (two or more).

Swedish has no polite you like Hindi आप or Marathi तुम्ही. Say du to one person, even a teacher, a doctor or a shop assistant. In Finland you may hear ni to one older stranger as extra politeness, but du is the normal choice.

Hen means one person without saying he or she, like English singular they. Use it when you do not know or it does not matter (En ny elev kommer. Hen heter Kim.), and for people who are neither he nor she. It works like Finnish hän. De (they, two or more) is written de but said dom.
Things are not han or hon. A thing is den or det (it): on page 6 the milk is den (Den är slut).
A common trap: someone and I together is vi (we). Anna och jag bor i Esbo. Vi talar svenska. When you talk to two people, use ni: Hej Sara och Peter! Talar ni svenska?

sections.title: People in your life: family and relationships
body: Family words are nouns: syster, bror, barn. Build sentences with the verbs har (have) and är (am, is, are): Jag har en syster. Jag är gift.

Swedish glues words together into compound words: pojke + vän = pojkvän (boyfriend), flicka + vän = flickvän (girlfriend). Bo means live, as in Jag bor i: a sambo lives together with a partner, a särbo lives apart.

Useful status words: gift (married), sambo, singel, skild (divorced; skilja sig = to get divorced), and Jag bor ensam (I live alone). Barn means child or children; syskon means brothers and sisters together.

examples.fi: Jag har en syster och en bror.
examples.en: I have a sister and a brother.
examples.note: En before one person: en syster, en bror.

examples.fi: Jag är sambo. Han heter Mikko.
examples.en: I live with my partner. His name is Mikko.
examples.note: Sambo: partners who live together without being married. Very common in Finland and Sweden.

examples.fi: Jag är gift. Jag har en fru.
examples.en: I'm married. I have a wife.
examples.note: Man = husband, fru = wife. Make and maka are formal words for spouse.

examples.fi: Jag är singel och jag bor ensam.
examples.en: I'm single and I live alone.
examples.note: Ensam = alone.

examples.fi: De har två barn, en son och en dotter.
examples.en: They have two children, a son and a daughter.
examples.note: Barn is both child and children. One child is ett barn, not en barn (en and ett come in a later lesson).

Jag är gift. Jag har en man.

sections.title: Question words: ask the next question
body: Vad = what, hur = how, var = where, varifrån = where from, när = when, varför = why, vem = who.

Word order: question word → verb → subject (the person). Var bor du? När kommer de? The verb comes second. If the question part is two words, like hur gammal, the verb comes right after both: Hur gammal är du?

English adds do: Where do you live? Swedish has no do. Var bor du? is word for word 'where live you'. Hindi puts the verb last (तुम कहाँ रहते हो?), but Swedish moves it up to second place. So never Var du bor?
A yes/no question starts with the verb itself: Är du gift? Har du syskon? Talar du svenska? You met Vilka språk talar du? in Lesson 1; vilken, vilket and vilka (which) come back in a later lesson.

sections.title: Hear it the way people say it
body: Written and spoken Swedish differ a little. Recognise these short forms now, and keep writing the full forms.
De is said dom. Jag is often just ja. Är often shrinks to e, det to de, and vad to va.
So Hur är det? often sounds like hur e de?, and De mår bra sounds like dom mår bra.

examples.fi: Vad heter du?

sections.memoryTip: Write it full, hear it short. When fast Swedish sounds strange, try the full form in your head.

assignment.title: Episode 2 mission: People in my life
assignment.instructions:
CORE: Answer Hur mår du? honestly and send it back with Och du? Then present two people in your life: who they are (Det är min …), their name (Hon heter … / Han heter …), and where they live.

QUESTION LOOP: Ask three questions with different question words, for example Var bor du? När kommer du? Varför pluggar du svenska? Keep the verb second.

RETURN: Without looking, say how you are and introduce one person in under 20 seconds.

Jag mår bra, tack. Och du?
Det är min syster. Hon heter Priya. Hon bor i Indien.

takeaways: Greet with Hej and Hur är det?, keep Hur mår du? for how someone really feels, then answer short and ask back: Bra, tack. Och du?
Pronouns: jag, du, han, hon, hen, vi, ni, de. Count the people for du and ni; write de but say dom.
Question word → verb → person: Var bor du? När kommer de?

pronunciation.text: Hur är det? Hur mår du? Toppen! Så där. Trött. Jag, du, han, hon, hen, vi, ni, de. Vad, hur, var, när, varför, vem.
pronunciation.tip: Choose one group. Hear the long, round å in mår and så, the open ä in är and när, and the ö in varför and trött. Say de as dom.

writing.prompt: Answer your friend's message: say how you are, ask back, tell her about one person in your life, and ask her one question.
writing.situation: Your friend Sara lives in Åbo. She sends you this message: “Hej! Hur mår du? Berätta om din familj!” (Hi! How are you? Tell me about your family!) Write back.
points: Say how you are, and ask how she is.
Tell her about one person in your life: who, their name, where they live.
Ask her one question with a question word (vad, var, när, varför, vem).
End with a greeting and your name.
writing.help: Hej Sara! · Jag mår bra / toppen / så där. · Hur mår du? · Jag har en syster / en bror / en vän. · Hon heter … / Han heter … · Hon bor i … · När kommer du till Helsingfors? · Hälsningar (Best wishes) and your name. Keep the verb second in your question.
